cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-gloria-in-excel.summary: For the Gloria in excelsis the artist drew the Trinity in the heavens: God the Father, beardless and holding a book, sits in a globe-mandorla; at his right the Virgin holds the cross-nimbed Christ child, with the dove of the Spirit above her, and on his other side stands the Lamb of God. Below, an angel gives palms to the 'men of good will'. Christ thus appears both as the Child and as the Lamb named in the hymn.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-gloria-in-excel.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-apostles-creed-.summary: For the Apostles' Creed the artist drew the Virgin holding the cross-nimbed Christ child about to set him on a cushioned globe at the right hand of God the Father, while the dove of the Spirit touches the child. The following articles of the Creed are pictured beside it: Christ brought before Pilate and the Crucifixion, with Christ in the colobium between the Virgin and Longinus, John and the sponge-bearer. It is the lower drawing of folio 90r.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.

The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-vault.summary: At the crown of the gold-covered vault, a bust of Christ in a blue medallion is held aloft by four white-robed angels who stand in the corners with arms raised, like caryatids of heaven. The whole small chapel seems to rise towards this image, so that those praying beneath stand under the gaze of Christ.
facts: The Chapel of Saint Zeno was built by Pope Paschal I (817–824) as a funerary chapel for his mother, Theodora; its walls and vault are almost entirely clad in gold-ground mosaic.
The four angels holding a medallion of Christ adapt an imperial and Ravennate motif, also found in the Archiepiscopal Chapel and San Vitale in Ravenna.
Paschal I's mosaics belong to the Carolingian-era revival in Rome, when the pope also translated many martyrs' relics from the catacombs into the city's churches.
